title: HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS)
subtitle: How a website tells your browser to never talk to it without encryption again.
summary: HSTS lets a website send a single HTTP response header, Strict-Transport-Security, telling browsers to use only HTTPS with that site for a stated number of seconds. During that time the browser upgrades plain http links itself and refuses to continue past certificate errors. This closes off downgrade and "click through the warning" attacks.

eli5.summary: A shop tells you once, "From now on, only come in through the locked front door, never the side door." You write it down, and for a long time you refuse the side door even if a stranger waves you over to it.

tldr.problem: Browsers happily start on plain HTTP and let users click through certificate warnings, so an attacker on the network can read cookies or impersonate the site.
tldr.mechanism: An HTTPS response carries Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=N. The browser remembers the host for N seconds, rewrites http URIs to https and treats every TLS error as fatal.
tldr.outcome: It protects every visit after the first and is supported by essentially all browsers, but it cannot protect a first-ever visit made over plain HTTP.

today: HSTS is one of the most widely deployed web security headers. Every major browser honours it, and most large sites and hosting platforms send it. Browser vendors also ship built-in "preload" lists of HSTS hosts, which is the kind of facility RFC 6797 section 12.3 describes, and site operators can ask to be added through the Chromium-maintained hstspreload.org service. You can see it in a browser's developer tools by looking at the response headers of any HTTPS page.

implementations.name: Web browsers
implementations.note: Chrome, Firefox, Safari and Edge all store HSTS policy and upgrade http URIs for known hosts.

implementations.name: hstspreload.org

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
HTTP by itself has no encryption, no integrity and no proof of who you are talking to. TLS, layered under HTTP as described in RFC 2818, adds all three. But a browser does not have to use it. A user can type http://, an old link can say http://, and when a certificate looks wrong, browsers have traditionally let the user press "continue anyway". The RFC calls this "click-through insecurity".

The danger is concrete. If a session cookie travels over even one plain-HTTP request, anyone on the same wireless network can copy it and become you. If the user clicks through a warning, an active attacker can sit in the middle of the connection.

RFC 6797 embodies and refines an earlier research proposal called ForceHTTPS. Instead of a cookie, the site conveys its wish using a new HTTP response header field, and the policy is applied to the entire host, over any TCP port.
sections.eli5: Some doors in the world are unlocked and some are locked, and people kept walking through the unlocked one by mistake. HSTS is a sign the shop hangs up that says: only use the locked door, and don't let anybody talk you out of it.

sections.title: Threats it addresses
sections.content:
The RFC names three threat classes it is meant to address, and two it explicitly is not.

Passive network attackers
Someone eavesdropping on a wireless network can steal session cookies sent in the clear. The RFC cites tools like Firesheep that did exactly this.
Active network attackers
An attacker who impersonates a DNS server or an access point can intercept HTTPS attempts and rely on users clicking through the resulting warning.
Site development bugs
One stylesheet or script loaded over plain HTTP can let an attacker take over an otherwise secure page.

HSTS is not a defense against phishing, where the user is lured to a different domain, and it cannot help if malware is already running on the user's machine.
sections.eli5: The sign protects you from someone listening at the wrong door, from someone pretending to be the shop, and from the shop accidentally leaving a side door open. It cannot stop you from walking into a completely different shop, or from a thief who is already inside your house.

sections.title: The mechanism
sections.content:
A site that wants HSTS returns one extra header over a secure connection. The browser (the RFC says "user agent") then notes the host as a Known HSTS Host, stores its domain name and an expiry time, and from then on does two things. It turns every insecure URI for that host into a secure one before loading it, and it ends any secure connection attempt that shows any error or warning at all, offering the user no way around it.

The policy is stored per domain name, and only the host itself can update or delete it, by sending a new header. Sending max-age=0 tells the browser to forget the host, including any includeSubDomains setting.

Two details matter for safety. A browser must only act on the header when it arrives over a secure transport with no errors, so an attacker cannot plant a policy through plain HTTP. And a host must never send the header over plain HTTP at all.
sections.eli5: The first time you visit over the locked door, the shop hands you a note: "For the next year, use only this door." You keep the note. Every time you plan to use the side door, you check your notes first and switch to the front door without asking anyone.

sections.title: The header and its directives
sections.content:
The syntax is a list of semicolon-separated directives, each a name with an optional value. The RFC defines two. Directive names are case-insensitive, the order does not matter, and each directive may appear only once.

max-age is required. Its value is a number of seconds, counted from when the header was received, for which the host is treated as a Known HSTS Host. The value may optionally be quoted. includeSubDomains is optional and has no value; when present, the policy covers the host and all of its subdomains.

The processing rules are deliberately strict. A browser MUST ignore a header that does not match the grammar, MUST ignore unknown directives while still processing the known ones, and, if a response carries more than one such header, MUST process only the first. The header is also ignored if it arrives over insecure transport, and a <meta http-equiv> version in page content must not be heeded.

Server operators are advised to default max-age to zero in their configuration systems, so that HSTS is only switched on by a deliberate choice of duration.
sections.eli5: The note has one required line (how long to remember) and one optional line (also applies to every little side shop on the same street). If the note is scribbled badly, you throw it away.

sections.title: What the browser does
sections.content:
Before loading any http URI, including when following a redirect, the browser extracts the host and checks it against its Known HSTS Hosts, comparing domain labels from right to left. IP addresses are never matched and never noted. A host matches if it is itself known (a congruent match), or if a known superdomain asserted includeSubDomains (a superdomain match).

On a match the browser replaces the scheme with https. If the URI carried an explicit port of 80 it becomes 443; any other explicit port is kept; if no port was written, none is added. Because the policy covers every port, a plain-HTTP service on port 8080 of a known host will simply fail.

An entry whose expiry has passed must be evicted. Responses from a known host that lack the header do not cancel the policy; it lasts until its max-age runs out.

Finally, on a known host the browser must abandon any connection with any TLS error, whether the error is labelled a warning or fatal. This includes certificate revocation and name checks, and the RFC advises "no user recourse" (no button to proceed).
sections.eli5: Before the browser goes anywhere, it checks its notes. If the shop (or the street the shop is on) is in the notes, it quietly swaps in the front door. And if the front door looks even slightly wrong, the browser simply refuses to go in, and does not ask you whether you want to.

sections.title: Deploying it safely
sections.content:
Section 11 is advice, not rules, and it exists because HSTS is easy to break your own site with. Choosing max-age means choosing between a constant window (for instance 7776000 seconds, 90 days, re-sent on each response) or a fixed end date, which needs a freshly computed value each time.

includeSubDomains protects "domain cookies" that apply to every subdomain, but it commits every subdomain to HTTPS. The RFC's example is a certificate authority that serves CRLs and OCSP over plain HTTP from a subdomain; an HSTS policy with includeSubDomains on the parent would make those fail.

Another trap: if a site redirects example.com to www.example.com and the header is sent only from the bare domain, visitors who go straight to www never learn the policy. The advice is to emit the header at every well-known entry point.

Organizations that issue certificates from their own CA should get that CA's root certificate trusted by their users' browsers before turning on HSTS, since certificate errors on an HSTS host cannot be clicked through. (The RFC also mentions TLSA as an alternative.)
sections.eli5: Writing "only the front door, for ten years, for every shop on the street" is powerful. If one of the shops on the street has no locked door, nobody will be able to get in. So shops are told to think carefully about how long a promise to make, and to put the sign up at every door people really use.

sections.title: Limits and security considerations
sections.content:
The RFC is frank about what HSTS cannot do.

Bootstrap problem. The first time a browser meets a host, it has no policy. If the user types or follows an http link, that first request is open to attack. The RFC suggests user-declared policies and browser-shipped "pre-loaded lists" to narrow this gap, but does not standardize either.

Time. Because policies expire, attackers who can fool a computer's clock through network time attacks can make HSTS less effective, particularly for clients that lack a real-time clock.

Denial of service. If an attacker can get an HSTS policy set on a host that actually serves content over plain HTTP, that content becomes unreachable for the victim. Inadvertent use of includeSubDomains can do the same by accident.

Tracking. Because hosts choose their own names and browsers cache them, a set of cleverly named hosts could encode a bit of information about whether a browser had visited. The RFC notes this as a possible web-tracking technique.

Finally, browsers that ignore the header (non-conformant user agents) get no protection from it.
sections.eli5: The note only helps after you've been given it. The very first time, you might still be tricked. A prankster might also trick you into writing a note for a shop that has no locked door, which would lock you out. And if someone fiddles with your clock, you might think the note has run out.

data.title: Strict-Transport-Security examples
data.code:
# One year, this host only
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000

# About six months, host and all subdomains
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=15768000 ; includeSubDomains

# max-age may be quoted
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age="31536000"

# Delete the policy (includeSubDomains is ignored when max-age is zero)
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=0

items.title: Start small
items.text: Default max-age to zero and set a duration deliberately.

items.title: Cover entry points
items.text: Send the header from every well-known host name, such as example.com and www.example.com.

items.title: Check subdomains first
items.text: includeSubDomains breaks any plain-HTTP service on a subdomain.

items.title: Redirect plain HTTP
items.text: Answer http requests with a permanent redirect such as 301 to https, but never send the header over plain HTTP.
